chapters.title: Make Python talk
chapters.desc: Start with output, quoted text, math, and the rules Python follows.

activities.title: Your first print()
activities.concept: print() tells Python to show something on the screen. The parentheses hold what you want to show.
activities.analogy: Think of print() as asking a tiny robot to say something out loud.
activities.task: Make the screen say: I wrote my first line!
activities.hint: Replace the words inside the quotes. Keep the matching quote marks.

activities.title: Math or text?
activities.concept: Without quotes, Python can calculate 2 + 5. With quotes, "2 + 5" is text. Quotes tell Python not to do the math.
activities.analogy: A math expression is a recipe to calculate. A string is a note containing characters that happen to look like math.
activities.task: Change the code so it prints the answer 7, not the characters 2 + 5.
activities.hint: Remove the quotes around 2 + 5. Keep print and its parentheses.

activities.title: Capital letters matter
activities.concept: Python is case-sensitive. print and Print are different names. The built-in command is all lowercase: print. Names like score and Score can also be different.
activities.analogy: Think of print and Print as two different passwords. One capital letter changes the spelling.
activities.example_code:
print("small letters work")
score = 8
Score = 2
print(score)
print(Score)
activities.task: Fix the code so it prints exactly: Python notices capitals.
activities.hint: Use lowercase print. A capital P is not the same command.

activities.title: Project: Intro card
activities.concept: Combine text and math in a tiny introduction. Each print makes a new line. Text needs quotes; math does not.
activities.analogy: It is like a mini poster built one line at a time.
activities.example_code:
print("Name: Lina")
print("Favorite subject: science")
print(2 + 5)
activities.task: Make a three-line card: name Noor, subject Art, and the answer to 10 + 4.
activities.hint: Fill the first two strings, then replace 0 with 10 + 4.
activities.solution_code:
print("Name: Noor")
print("Favorite subject: Art")
print(10 + 4)

chapters.title: Store information
chapters.desc: Give values names so your program can remember and reuse them.

activities.title: Create a variable
activities.concept: A variable is a name connected to a value. The single equals sign assigns the value on its right to the name on its left.
activities.analogy: A variable is like a labelled box: score is the label and 12 is what is inside.
activities.task: Make a variable called stars with the value 5, then print it.
activities.hint: Change the value after the equals sign. Do not put quotes around the number.

activities.title: Choose useful names
activities.concept: Names can use letters, numbers, and underscores, but cannot start with a number. Names cannot contain spaces. Python keywords such as if are reserved.
activities.analogy: A useful variable name is a clear label. total_points tells you more than x.
activities.task: Create game_level with the value 3 and print it.
activities.hint: Keep the name exactly game_level and change its number to 3.

activities.title: Update a value
activities.concept: You can assign a new value to an existing variable. Python reads the right side first, then stores the result under the name on the left.
activities.analogy: It is like crossing out the old number on a whiteboard and writing a new one.
activities.task: Start with 10 points, add 6 more using the variable itself, and print 16.
activities.hint: Replace + 0 with + 6. Python uses the old value first.

activities.title: Project: Score keeper
activities.concept: Use variables to store, update, and display a game score.
activities.analogy: It is like keeping score in a notebook, but Python updates it for you.
activities.task: Make the starting score 7, add 8, and print Final score: 15.
activities.hint: Set the first value to 7 and the added value to 8.

chapters.title: Numbers and math
chapters.desc: Use arithmetic, parentheses, remainders, and rounding.

activities.title: Add and subtract
activities.concept: Use + to add and - to subtract. Python calculates numbers when they are not inside quotes.
activities.analogy: The symbols work like the calculator you already know.
activities.task: Print 30 minus 12.
activities.hint: Replace the zeros with 30 and 12.

activities.title: Multiply and divide
activities.concept: Use * for multiplication and / for division. In Python, multiplication is an asterisk, not the letter x.
activities.analogy: The computer uses keyboard-friendly symbols. * means times.
activities.task: Print the result of 8 times 9.
activities.hint: Use * and numbers without quote marks.

activities.title: Order of operations
activities.concept: Python follows math order: parentheses first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.
activities.analogy: Parentheses are like saying, “Do this part first.”
activities.task: Make Python calculate (6 + 2) times 3.
activities.hint: Put parentheses around 6 + 2.

activities.title: Remainders with %
activities.concept: The % operator gives the remainder after division. 17 % 5 is 2 because 5 fits three times into 17 and 2 are left.
activities.analogy: Imagine sharing 17 biscuits with 5 people. The remainder is what is left after equal groups.
activities.task: Print the remainder when 23 is divided by 4.
activities.hint: Change the divisor from 1 to 4. Five groups use 20, leaving 3.

activities.title: Project: Mini shop total
activities.concept: Calculate a shopping total using multiplication and addition.
activities.analogy: A checkout multiplies item price by quantity, then adds prices together.
activities.task: A notebook costs 4 and you buy 3. Print Total: 12.
activities.hint: Use quantity 3 and keep price 4.

chapters.title: Text and strings
chapters.desc: Join text, change letter case, and put values inside messages.

activities.title: Text is called a string
activities.concept: A string is text surrounded by matching quotes. Python keeps the characters inside the quotes, including spaces and punctuation.
activities.analogy: A string is a strip of text. Quote marks show where that strip starts and ends.
activities.task: Print the exact text: I like Python!
activities.hint: Replace the words inside the quotes. Keep the quote marks.

activities.title: Join strings with +
activities.concept: The + operator joins two strings. This is called concatenation. It does not add a space automatically.
activities.analogy: Tape two labels together. Add a space yourself if you want one between the words.
activities.task: Join code and time with a space between them.
activities.hint: Add a string containing one space between the two words.

activities.title: Change text case
activities.concept: String methods such as .upper() and .lower() return text in a different letter case. The parentheses call the method.
activities.analogy: It is like changing a sign from lowercase to uppercase.
activities.task: Print learn in uppercase.
activities.hint: Add .upper() after the closing quote.

activities.title: Build messages with f-strings
activities.concept: Put f before the opening quote, then place a variable or expression inside curly braces. Python replaces the braces with the value.
activities.analogy: An f-string is a fill-in-the-blank sentence. Curly braces show where Python should put the answer.
activities.task: Use an f-string to print Ava is 14.
activities.hint: Put f before the quote and {age} where the number should appear.

activities.title: Project: Personalized badge
activities.concept: Build a name badge by combining strings, variables, and an f-string.
activities.analogy: A name badge takes stored information and displays it in a readable format.
activities.task: Make the output say Welcome, Rami! Level 2 using an f-string.
activities.hint: Use f-string placeholders for nickname and level.

chapters.title: Types and conversions
chapters.desc: Learn the difference between numbers, text, and converting values.

activities.title: Numbers and text are different types
activities.concept: int means whole number, float means a number that may have a decimal, and str means text. type(value) tells you a value type.
activities.analogy: The characters 12 and the number 12 look alike, but they behave differently.
activities.task: Print the type of 3.5.
activities.hint: Use the decimal number 3.5.

activities.title: Turn text into a number
activities.concept: int("12") converts numeric text to a whole number. float("3.5") converts numeric text to a decimal. Invalid text can cause ValueError.
activities.analogy: Text saying 12 is like a label. Conversion changes it into a number Python can calculate with.
activities.task: Convert the text 8 to an integer, add 2, and print 10.
activities.hint: Change + 0 to + 2. The conversion is already done.

activities.title: Turn a value into text
activities.concept: str(value) turns a value into text. This is useful when you want to join a number with a string using +.
activities.analogy: You turn a number into printable writing before attaching it to a sentence.
activities.task: Print Level 3 by joining the text Level and the number 3 converted to text.
activities.hint: Use str(level) so Python joins two strings.

activities.title: Project: Age next year
activities.concept: Use a text value, convert it to a number, then calculate next year’s age.
activities.analogy: A form often gives you text, but math needs a number. Convert before calculating.
activities.task: The text is 15. Convert it and print Next year: 16.
activities.hint: Add one to age inside the f-string.

chapters.title: Ask the user for input
chapters.desc: Make programs respond to information typed by the person running them.

activities.title: input() reads what someone types
activities.concept: input() pauses and returns the answer as text. Save the answer in a variable to use it later.
activities.analogy: The program asks a question and waits for the person to reply.
activities.task: Ask for a name and greet the person. Test input is Noor.
activities.hint: Keep the question and change the second line to an f-string greeting.

activities.title: Convert input into a whole number
activities.concept: Input is text, even when the person types digits. Use int(input(...)) to read a whole number for calculations.
activities.analogy: The user hands you a number written on paper; int() reads it as a number.
activities.task: Ask for a number and print it multiplied by 2. Test input is 6.
activities.hint: Wrap input in int(), then multiply by 2.

activities.title: Use float() for decimal input
activities.concept: Use float(input(...)) when someone may enter a decimal such as 2.5. Use int() for whole numbers.
activities.analogy: A measuring scale can include fractions, so decimals need float().
activities.task: Read a decimal and add 1.0. Test input is 3.5.
activities.hint: Convert the input to float, then add 1.0.

activities.title: Project: Snack order
activities.concept: Ask the person for a snack and how many they want, then show the order.
activities.analogy: A simple order form asks for choices, stores them, then repeats them clearly.
activities.example_code:
snack = input("Snack? ")
count = int(input("How many? "))
print(f"Order: {count} {snack}")
activities.example_output:
Snack? apple
How many? 3
Order: 3 apple
activities.task: Make an order for 2 cookies. Use the provided two input lines.
activities.starter_code:
snack = input("Snack? ")
count = int(input("How many? "))
print("Order ready")
activities.expected_output:
Snack? cookies
How many? 2
Order: 2 cookies
activities.hint: Use an f-string with both count and snack.
activities.solution_code:
snack = input("Snack? ")
count = int(input("How many? "))
print(f"Order: {count} {snack}")

chapters.title: True or False checks
chapters.desc: Compare values and combine yes-or-no answers with Boolean logic.

activities.title: Comparisons answer a question
activities.concept: == checks whether values are equal. != checks whether they differ. <, >, <=, and >= compare sizes.
activities.analogy: A comparison is like asking a yes-or-no question. Python answers with True or False.
activities.task: Print whether 12 is at least 12.
activities.hint: Use >= because equal values count too.

activities.title: True and False use capitals
activities.concept: Python Boolean values are exactly True and False, with capital first letters. true and false are not the same names.
activities.analogy: The capital letter is part of the exact spelling of these special values.
activities.task: Create a Boolean called is_ready with the value True and print it.
activities.hint: Change False to True with a capital T.

activities.title: Combine checks with and, or, not
activities.concept: and needs both checks to be true. or needs at least one check to be true. not flips a Boolean value.
activities.analogy: A game door might require a key and a ticket. Another door might allow either one of two passes.
activities.example_code:
print(True and False)
print(True or False)
print(not True)
activities.task: Print True when score is 80 and it is between 60 and 100. Use and.
activities.hint: Combine score >= 60 and score <= 100 with and.

activities.title: Project: Game eligibility
activities.concept: Combine age and permission checks into a yes-or-no result.
activities.analogy: A game can check two requirements before opening a level.
activities.example_code:
age = 14
has_key = True
print(age >= 13 and has_key)
activities.task: Check that score is at least 50 and the player has a pass. Use score 76 and has_pass True.
activities.hint: The final answer needs both the score comparison and has_pass.
activities.solution_code:
score = 76
has_pass = True
print(score >= 50 and has_pass)

chapters.title: Make decisions with if
chapters.desc: Use if, elif, else, and indentation to choose what your program does.

activities.title: if runs code only when true
activities.concept: if condition: runs the indented block only when the condition is true. The colon starts the block and indentation shows which lines belong to it.
activities.analogy: It is a rule: if it is raining, take an umbrella.
activities.task: Print Ready only when energy is greater than 0.
activities.hint: Change the message to Ready. Keep print indented under if.

activities.title: else handles the other case
activities.concept: else runs when the if condition is false. It has a colon and no condition after it.
activities.analogy: If the bus is here, get on; otherwise, wait.
activities.task: Use if/else to print Even when a number is even and Odd otherwise.
activities.hint: The first message should be Even. Seven takes the else branch.

activities.title: elif checks another possibility
activities.concept: elif means else if. Python checks conditions in order and runs only the first matching branch.
activities.analogy: It is like checking a list of rules from top to bottom and stopping at the first that fits.
activities.task: For points 12, print Gold at 15 or more, Silver at 10 or more, otherwise Bronze.
activities.hint: Change the second branch message to Silver.

activities.title: Project: Adventure choice
activities.concept: Build a mini adventure that chooses a message based on the player’s health.
activities.analogy: A game reacts differently depending on a player’s current state.
activities.task: Print Safe for health above 10, Careful for health above 0, and Game over for 0.
activities.hint: Change the middle branch to Careful.

chapters.title: Lists of things
chapters.desc: Create lists, pick items by index, add items, and use built-in helpers.

activities.title: Make a list
activities.concept: A list stores several values in one ordered collection, using square brackets and commas.
activities.analogy: A list is a row of slots. Each slot keeps one item in order.
activities.task: Make a list of 3, 5, and 8, then print it.
activities.hint: Use square brackets and commas: [3, 5, 8].

activities.title: Indexes start at zero
activities.concept: Use an index inside square brackets to get an item. The first index is 0, the second is 1, and so on.
activities.analogy: The first seat in a Python queue has index zero.
activities.task: Print the second item in animals = fox, owl, bear.
activities.hint: The second item uses index 1, not 2.

activities.title: Append and count items
activities.concept: append(item) adds one item to the end of a list. len(list) counts its items.
activities.analogy: Appending is placing another card at the end of the row. len counts the cards.
activities.task: Append sleep to [eat, play] and print the full list.
activities.hint: Change the appended item to sleep.

activities.title: Use sum() and sorted()
activities.concept: sum(numbers) adds a numeric list. sorted(items) makes a sorted list and leaves the original list unchanged.
activities.analogy: sum is like adding every score. sorted puts the cards in order.
activities.task: Print the total of [2, 4, 6], then its sorted list.
activities.hint: Add print(sorted(values)) after the sum.

activities.title: Project: Playlist manager
activities.concept: Store a short playlist, add a song, and show the list length.
activities.analogy: A playlist is a collection you can grow and count.
activities.task: Create songs Sky and Ocean, append Stars, then print the list and its length.
activities.hint: Start with both Sky and Ocean, append Stars, then print the list and its length.

chapters.title: Repeat with for loops
chapters.desc: Make Python repeat a task without copying the same line many times.

activities.title: Loop through a list
activities.concept: A for loop runs its indented block once for each item in a list. The loop variable takes the current item each time.
activities.analogy: A loop is like going through a checklist and doing the same action for every row.
activities.task: Print each number in [2, 4, 6] on its own line.
activities.hint: Replace the list with [2, 4, 6].

activities.title: Count with range()
activities.concept: range(5) gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The stop value is not included. range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3, 4.
activities.analogy: range is a number ticket dispenser that stops just before the ending number.
activities.task: Print 1, 2, 3, 4 using range().
activities.hint: The stop number should be 5 because it is excluded.

activities.title: Keep a running total
activities.concept: A variable can collect a running total. Give it a starting value before the loop, then update it each time.
activities.analogy: A running total is like a cash register adding each item as it passes.
activities.example_code:
total = 0
for value in [2, 3, 4]:
    total = total + value
print(total)
activities.task: Use a loop to add 1, 2, and 3, then print 6.
activities.starter_code:
total = 0
for value in [1, 2, 3]:
    total = total + value
print(total)
activities.hint: This starter has the right pattern. Make sure the total prints after the loop.
activities.solution_code:
total = 0
for value in [1, 2, 3]:
    total = total + value
print(total)

activities.title: Project: Multiplication table
activities.concept: Use a loop to print multiplication facts in a predictable pattern.
activities.analogy: A loop fills out each row in a table without repeated code.
activities.task: Print 5, 10, 15, 20 by multiplying numbers 1 through 4 by five.
activities.hint: Use range(1, 5) so the loop visits 1, 2, 3, and 4.

chapters.title: While loops and loop control
chapters.desc: Repeat while a condition is true and learn how to stop safely.

activities.title: Repeat while true
activities.concept: A while loop repeats while its condition is true. Update the variable inside the loop so the condition can eventually become false.
activities.analogy: It is like saying “keep going while the timer is above zero.”
activities.example_code:
count = 1
while count <= 3:
    print(count)
    count = count + 1
activities.task: Print 1 and 2 using a while loop.
activities.starter_code:
count = 1
while count <= 1:
    print(count)
    count = count + 1
activities.hint: Change <= 1 to <= 2 so it can reach 2.
activities.solution_code:
count = 1
while count <= 2:
    print(count)
    count = count + 1

activities.title: Avoid an infinite loop
activities.concept: An infinite loop never reaches a stopping condition. If the condition is always true and nothing changes it, the program can run forever.
activities.analogy: It is like walking in a circle without a plan to stop.
activities.task: Make the loop print 0, 1, 2 and stop.
activities.hint: Update count inside the loop, for example with count += 1.

activities.title: break and continue
activities.concept: break exits a loop early. continue skips the rest of the current turn and moves to the next one.
activities.analogy: break is an emergency exit. continue skips to the next page in a checklist.
activities.task: Print 1, 2, and 4, skipping 3 with continue.
activities.hint: Add an if number == 3 block with an indented continue before print.

activities.title: Project: Countdown
activities.concept: Use a while loop to count down and finish with Launch!.
activities.analogy: A countdown repeats while the number is above zero.
activities.example_code:
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count -= 1
print("Go!")
activities.task: Make a countdown from 4 to 1 and then print Launch!.
activities.starter_code:
count = 2
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count -= 1
print("Go!")
activities.hint: Start at 4 and change the final message to Launch!.
activities.solution_code:
count = 4
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count -= 1
print("Launch!")

chapters.title: Write reusable functions
chapters.desc: Put a named set of instructions in one place and call it whenever you need it.

activities.title: Define a function
activities.concept: Use def name(): to define a function. The indented lines form its body. The body does not run until the function is called.
activities.analogy: A function is a named recipe card. Writing the recipe is not the same as cooking it.
activities.task: Define cheer() so it prints You can do it!, then call it.
activities.hint: Change the message inside the function.

activities.title: Call a function more than once
activities.concept: After a function is defined, you can call it many times using its name and parentheses.
activities.analogy: Once you have a recipe, you can cook it more than once without rewriting it.
activities.task: Call wave() twice so Hello! prints twice.
activities.hint: Add a second call to wave() on a new line.

activities.title: Indent the function body
activities.concept: Python uses indentation to show which instructions belong to the function. Bad indentation can cause an error.
activities.analogy: The function body is like recipe steps under the recipe title.
activities.task: Make start_game() print Start and Play fair on separate lines.
activities.starter_code:
def start_game():
print("Start")
    print("Play fair")
start_game()
activities.hint: Indent both print lines by four spaces.
activities.solution_code:
def start_game():
    print("Start")
    print("Play fair")
start_game()

activities.title: Project: Reusable cheer
activities.concept: Write one function and use it several times.
activities.analogy: Instead of copying a message, you call your named recipe.
activities.task: Create level_up() that prints Level up!, then call it twice.
activities.hint: Change the message and add a second function call.
activities.solution_code:
def level_up():
    print("Level up!")
level_up()
level_up()

chapters.title: Functions with inputs and results
chapters.desc: Give functions parameters and send information back with return.

activities.title: Parameters receive values
activities.concept: A parameter is a name in the function definition. The argument is the real value passed when you call the function.
activities.analogy: A function with a parameter is like a machine with an input slot.
activities.task: Make the function greet the name Noor.
activities.hint: Change the argument inside greet(...) from Sam to Noor.

activities.title: return sends a result back
activities.concept: return sends a value back to the code that called the function. You can use the result in a variable or another expression.
activities.analogy: A function can be a calculator: it takes inputs and hands back an answer.
activities.example_code:
def double(number):
    return number * 2
answer = double(6)
print(answer)
activities.task: Write triple(number) that returns number times 3. Call it with 4 and print 12.
activities.hint: Change the return line so it multiplies number by 3.

activities.title: return is not print
activities.concept: print displays a value. return sends a value back to the caller. A function can return a result without displaying it.
activities.analogy: print is a loudspeaker; return passes a note back to whoever asked.
activities.example_code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b
result = add(2, 3)
print(result)
activities.task: Create area(width, height) that returns width times height. Print area(3, 4).
activities.hint: Return the product width * height.

activities.title: Project: Discount calculator
activities.concept: Create a function that calculates a price after a discount.
activities.analogy: A reusable calculator keeps the formula in one place.
activities.task: Write discounted(price) that returns price minus 3. Print the result for 12.
activities.hint: Subtract 3 from price in the return expression.

chapters.title: Dictionaries
chapters.desc: Store related information using named keys instead of numeric indexes.

activities.title: Create a dictionary
activities.concept: A dictionary stores key-value pairs inside curly braces. A key such as name helps you find its value.
activities.analogy: A dictionary is like a contact card: the label name points to the person’s name.
activities.task: Create a dictionary with key color and value blue, then print the value.
activities.hint: Change the value from red to blue. Keep the key color the same.

activities.title: Add or change a value
activities.concept: Assign to dictionary[key] to add a new pair or replace a value stored under that key.
activities.analogy: A dictionary lets you update information on a named card.
activities.task: Change the score to 25 and print it.
activities.hint: Assign 25 to player["score"].

activities.title: Use get() for a safe default
activities.concept: get(key, default) returns a default value when the key is missing. Direct lookup with a missing key raises KeyError.
activities.analogy: A default is a backup answer when a dictionary has no entry for a key.
activities.task: Print unknown as the default for a missing pet key.
activities.hint: Change the fallback string from cat to unknown.

activities.title: Project: Player profile
activities.concept: Build and update a game profile with related values.
activities.analogy: One dictionary stores information about a player in a clear structure.
activities.task: Make a profile for Kai at level 4, then print Kai level 4.
activities.hint: Use an f-string that reads both dictionary values.

chapters.title: Errors and debugging
chapters.desc: Read error messages, check assumptions, and handle expected problems.

activities.title: Read the error name first
activities.concept: SyntaxError means code cannot be understood. NameError means a name was not found. TypeError means an operation does not fit the value type.
activities.analogy: An error message is a clue from the computer, not a grade. Start by reading its name and line number.
activities.task: Fix this program so it prints 5.0 instead of dividing by zero.
activities.hint: Use division by 2 instead of 0. Python’s / operator produces a decimal-style float.

activities.title: Fix a NameError
activities.concept: Names must be spelled consistently and defined before use. score and Score are different because Python notices capitals.
activities.analogy: A name is like a contact saved under an exact spelling. One wrong letter points to nobody.
activities.task: Fix the code so it prints 9 without a NameError.
activities.hint: The name in print must exactly match points.

activities.title: Fix a TypeError
activities.concept: A TypeError happens when an operation does not make sense for the types. For example, joining text and an integer needs conversion or an f-string.
activities.analogy: You cannot add an apple to a number on a calculator. Convert or choose an operation that fits.
activities.task: Fix this so it prints Next year: 15.
activities.hint: Convert the numeric result to text with str(...) or use an f-string.

activities.title: Handle an expected error
activities.concept: A try block contains code that might fail. An except block describes what to do if a matching error happens.
activities.analogy: try/except is like having a backup plan for a predictable problem.
activities.task: Try converting hello and print Please use digits if it causes ValueError.
activities.hint: Change 7 to hello and change the error message.

activities.title: Project: Safe number reader
activities.concept: Build a number reader that handles non-number input without crashing.
activities.analogy: Good programs plan for mistakes people can make while typing.
activities.task: Attempt to convert oops to int. On ValueError, print Invalid number.
activities.hint: Use oops and change the except message.

chapters.title: Tools and bigger ideas
chapters.desc: Use modules, solve simple data problems, and build your own objects.

activities.title: Import math
activities.concept: import math makes the math module available. You can use math.sqrt() to calculate a square root.
activities.analogy: A module is a toolbox. Importing it gives you access to tools someone already built.
activities.task: Use math.sqrt to print the square root of 144.
activities.hint: Replace 9 with 144.

activities.title: Count matching items
activities.concept: A loop and an if can count how many items match a rule. Start the counter at zero and increase it when the rule is true.
activities.analogy: It is like checking each answer and adding a tally for each match.
activities.task: Count how many numbers are greater than 5 in [2, 8, 9, 1].
activities.hint: Change the condition to number > 5. Eight and nine match.

activities.title: Make a simple class
activities.concept: A class describes a kind of object. An object can store information in attributes and provide actions through methods.
activities.analogy: A class is a blueprint. Objects are things built from that blueprint.
activities.example_code:
class Pet:
    pass
pet = Pet()
print(type(pet).__name__)
activities.task: Create a class named Robot, make one object, and print its type name.
activities.starter_code:
class Robot:
    pass
bot = Robot()
print(type(bot).__name__)
activities.hint: The class name and __name__ should both be Robot.
activities.solution_code:
class Robot:
    pass
bot = Robot()
print(type(bot).__name__)

activities.title: Project: Pet simulator
activities.concept: Use a class to store a pet’s name and happiness, then change its happiness with a method.
activities.analogy: The object keeps both the pet’s details and actions it can perform.
activities.task: Create pet Luna, play twice, and print Luna: 2.
activities.hint: Call pet.play() a second time.
